source.name: VocabBuilder starter set (Brazilian Portuguese)
source.notes: Hand-written by an AI assistant (Claude) as a small starter set for VocabBuilder. Not corpus-derived: curatedOrder is a teaching order, not a frequency rank. Review and edit freely.

senses.note: As an answer or reply: Tudo bem! = I'm fine / It's OK / No problem.

entries.regionalNote: The everyday Brazilian greeting. Casual variants: Tudo bom? / Tudo certo? / Beleza?

senses.note: Used until about noon; then boa tarde (good afternoon) and boa noite (good evening, good night).

examples.translation: Good morning! Did you sleep well?
Thanks so much for the help!

grammar.notes: Agrees with the speaker: men say obrigado, women say obrigada.

entries.regionalNote: Among friends Brazilians often just say Valeu! (Thanks!, informal).

examples.text: Pode falar mais devagar, por favor?
examples.translation: Could you speak more slowly, please?
You're welcome, it was a pleasure.

examples.text: Imagina, de nada! Precisando, é só falar.
examples.translation: Don't mention it! If you need anything, just ask.

entries.regionalNote: Brazilians also reply Imagina! (Don't mention it!) or Por nada.

examples.translation: Yes, of course! Come on in.

grammar.notes: Brazilians often answer 'yes' by repeating the verb instead: Você quer café? — Quero!

senses.note: Before a verb it means 'not': Não entendi (I didn't understand).

grammar.notes: In speech it is often repeated at the end for emphasis: Não sei, não (I really don't know).

examples.translation: Do you guys want to grab a coffee?

grammar.notes: Takes the same verb form as ele/ela: você fala, você é. Plural vocês = you all. To show respect (older people, formal settings): o senhor / a senhora.

entries.regionalNote: Standard in most of Brazil; in speech often shortened to cê. In some regions (the South, Rio, parts of the North and Northeast) you'll also hear tu.

senses.note: Colloquial 'we', extremely common in speech; 'us' after prepositions: com a gente (with us).

examples.text: Você quer almoçar com a gente?
examples.translation: Do you want to have lunch with us?

grammar.notes: Takes the 3rd-person singular verb form: a gente vai (we're going), a gente é. Without the article, gente means 'people' or 'guys': Oi, gente!

entries.regionalNote: Used all over Brazil in everyday speech; nós sounds more formal or written.

senses.note: Identity, origin, profession and characteristics: Sou de Chicago.

grammar.notes: Irregular. Ser for identity, origin and characteristics; estar for location and temporary states. Você and a gente take the ele form: você é, a gente é.

senses.note: Location and temporary states: Estou cansado.

grammar.notes: Irregular. In speech often shortened: tô (estou), tá (está), tão (estão).

senses.note: Brazilian everyday use of tem: Tem pão? (Is there any bread?)

examples.text: Eu tenho uma irmã mais velha.

examples.translation: Is there a pharmacy near here?

grammar.notes: Irregular: tenho, tem, past teve. Note the circumflex in vocês/eles têm.

entries.regionalNote: In Brazil tem is the everyday way to say 'there is/are'; há (from haver) sounds formal or written.

examples.text: Você quer sair hoje à noite?
examples.translation: Do you want to go out tonight?

examples.text: Eu queria um suco de manga.

grammar.notes: Irregular: ele quer (no final -e), past quis. For polite requests use the imperfect: Eu queria… (I'd like…).

examples.text: Eu vou ao mercado mais tarde.
examples.translation: I'm going to the supermarket later.
Shall we go get an açaí?

grammar.notes: Very irregular. Ir + infinitive = 'going to': Vou comer. The past foi is the same as for ser.

examples.text: Uma água sem gás, por favor.

examples.translation: Would you like a glass of water?
I drink my coffee without sugar.

entries.regionalNote: A cafezinho (small, strong, often sweet coffee) is offered to guests and clients all over Brazil.

grammar.notes: Irregular: eu posso. The past pôde has a circumflex to distinguish it from the present pode.

examples.translation: Do you speak English or Spanish?

examples.text: Eu falo um pouco de português.

grammar.notes: Regular -ar verb.

examples.text: Você entendeu o que eu falei?
examples.translation: Did you understand what I said?

examples.text: Eu entendo, mas não falo bem.
examples.translation: I understand, but I don't speak well.

grammar.notes: Regular -er verb. Não entendi = I didn't understand / I didn't get that.

examples.text: Onde fica a estação de metrô?

examples.translation: Where did you buy that T-shirt?

grammar.notes: For the location of places use Onde fica…? (Where is…?). 'Where to' is para onde: Para onde você vai?
As an adverb it never changes. Before a noun it agrees like an adjective: muita gente (a lot of people), muitos amigos (lots of friends).
lá = there; ali = over there.

examples.text: Vem aqui em casa no sábado!
examples.translation: Come over to my place on Saturday!

grammar.notes: em casa = at home; para casa = (to) home.

examples.text: Eu vou de metrô para o trabalho.
examples.translation: I take the subway to work.

grammar.notes: The verb is trabalhar (to work). A job is also emprego: Estou procurando emprego.

examples.text: Qual é o seu número de celular?

senses.note: Common slang: grana (Tô sem grana = I'm broke).

examples.translation: I'm out of money this month.
Do you take cards or just cash?

grammar.notes: Uncountable, like English 'money': muito dinheiro (a lot of money).

examples.text: Com licença, onde fica o banheiro?

examples.translation: Do you have an account at this bank?

expressions.translation: to ask for and settle the bill

examples.translation: Shall we get something to eat?

grammar.notes: Regular -er verb.

senses.note: The everyday verb for drinks: tomar um café, tomar uma cerveja.
tomar banho = to take a shower; tomar remédio = to take medicine.

examples.text: Vou tomar banho e já volto.
examples.translation: I'm going to take a shower, I'll be right back.

grammar.notes: Regular -ar verb.
Always followed by de: gosto de café, gosto do Brasil (de + o = do).

examples.text: O que você vai fazer hoje?

grammar.notes: Irregular: faço, faz, past fez. Weather: faz calor / faz frio (it's hot / cold). Time ago: faz dois anos (two years ago).

senses.note: Where you live (your home). Viver = to live in the sense of being alive or experiencing.

examples.text: Eu moro em São Paulo há dois anos.
examples.translation: I've lived in São Paulo for two years.
Do you guys live near here?

grammar.notes: Regular -ar verb. Onde você mora? = Where do you live?
precisar de + noun (Preciso de ajuda); no de before an infinitive (Preciso ir).

senses.note: Transport: pegar o ônibus, pegar um Uber.

examples.text: Vou pegar um táxi para o aeroporto.
examples.translation: I'm going to take a taxi to the airport.

examples.text: Eu te pego no hotel às oito.
examples.translation: I'll pick you up at the hotel at eight.

grammar.notes: Regular -ar verb; pego, pega and pegam have an open e (é).

examples.text: Agora não posso, estou no trabalho.
examples.translation: I can't right now, I'm at work.

examples.text: Hoje à noite a gente sai.

grammar.notes: de manhã = in the morning; a manhã = the morning.

examples.text: É caro, mas é muito bom.
examples.translation: It's expensive, but it's really good.

examples.text: Eu queria ir, mas não posso.
examples.translation: I'd like to go, but I can't.

grammar.notes: Don't confuse it with mais (more).
Masculine despite ending in -a: o dia, bom dia.

examples.text: A gente se fala semana que vem.

examples.translation: I work five days a week.
Do you know what time it is?
I'll be there in an hour.

grammar.notes: The time is asked in the plural: Que horas são? (What time is it?)

senses.note: Informal: cara (dude, guy) is used all over Brazil: E aí, cara?

examples.text: Vou sair com uns amigos hoje.
examples.translation: I'm going out with some friends today.

examples.text: Ele é uma pessoa muito legal.

examples.translation: There were lots of people at the party.

grammar.notes: Always feminine, even when it refers to a man: Ele é uma pessoa ótima.
Irregular: bom, boa, bons, boas. Comparative: melhor (better).

senses.note: Of people it means 'nice': Ele é muito legal. It can also mean 'legal' (lawful).

examples.text: Que legal! Parabéns pelo emprego novo!
examples.translation: That's great! Congrats on the new job!

grammar.notes: Same form for masculine and feminine; plural legais.

entries.regionalNote: Very Brazilian in the sense of 'cool' or 'nice'; in Portugal you'd say fixe.

senses.note: Also 'pleasant' for things like a breeze or a shower. Said of a person, gostoso/gostosa means 'hot, sexy', so keep it for food and things.

examples.text: A comida da sua mãe é gostosa.
A feira é mais barata que o mercado.
examples.translation: The street market is cheaper than the supermarket.

examples.text: Você conhece um hotel barato por aqui?
examples.translation: Do you know a cheap hotel around here?

grammar.notes: Careful: the noun a barata means 'cockroach'.

examples.translation: What a beautiful day today, huh?

grammar.notes: Same form for masculine and feminine.

examples.text: Meu apartamento é pequeno, mas é confortável.
examples.translation: My apartment is small, but it's comfortable.

grammar.notes: In speech Brazilians often use diminutives instead: um cafezinho, uma casinha.

examples.text: Esse ônibus vai para o centro?
Eu pego o ônibus na esquina.
examples.translation: I catch the bus on the corner.

grammar.notes: Same form in the plural: um ônibus, dois ônibus.

examples.text: Vamos de carro ou de ônibus?
examples.translation: Are we going by car or by bus?
Where did you park the car?

examples.text: O café da manhã está incluído?
No café da manhã eu como pão com manteiga.
examples.translation: For breakfast I have bread and butter.

grammar.notes: Masculine: o café da manhã. To have breakfast = tomar café da manhã (often just tomar café).

expressions.translation: set lunch plate: rice, beans, meat and salad

grammar.notes: The verb is almoçar (to have lunch).

examples.text: A comida daqui é muito boa.
examples.translation: The food here is really good.
Do you like food from Minas Gerais?

examples.text: Vou passar na padaria para comprar pão.
examples.translation: I'm going to stop by the bakery to buy bread.

expressions.translation: cheese bread (small cheese rolls from Minas Gerais)

grammar.notes: Irregular plural: pães.

examples.text: Um suco de laranja, por favor.
O suco de maracujá aqui é ótimo.
examples.translation: The passion fruit juice here is great.
Shall we go to the beach on Sunday?
